# M5 gate (a): spoken form of every equation segment and inline-maths sentence, convention spec 3c
p equals the probability of a success for any trial
q equals the probability of a failure for any trial
p plus q equals 1
q equals 1 minus p
the mean of x is mu equals n p.
the standard deviation of x is sigma equals the square root of n p q.
x distributed as g of p means that the discrete random variable x has a geometric probability distribution with probability of success in a single trial p.
x equals the number of independent trials until the first success
x takes on the values x equals 1, 2, 3, ...
p equals the probability of a success for any trial
q equals the probability of a failure for any trial p plus q equals 1
q equals 1 minus p
the mean is mu equals 1 over p.
the standard deviation is sigma equals the square root of the fraction 1 minus p over p squared, end fraction equals the square root of 1 over p times 1 over p minus 1.
x distributed as h of r, b and n means that the discrete random variable x has a hypergeometric probability distribution with r equals the size of the group of interest first group, b equals the size of the second group, and n equals the size of the chosen sample.
x equals the number of items from the group of interest that are in the chosen sample, and x may take on the values x equals 0, 1, ..., up to the size of the group of interest.
the minimum value for x may be larger than zero in some instances.
n is less than or equal to r plus b
the mean of x is given by the formula mu equals the fraction n r over r plus b, end fraction and the standard deviation is equals the square root of the fraction r b n times r plus b minus n over r plus b squared times r plus b minus 1, end fraction.
x distributed as p of mu means that x has a poisson probability distribution where x equals the number of occurrences in the interval of interest.
x takes on the values x equals 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
the mean mu is typically given.
the variance is sigma squared equals mu, and the standard deviation is sigma equals the square root of mu.
when p of mu is used to approximate a binomial distribution, mu equals n p where n represents the number of independent trials and p represents the probability of success in a single trial.
let x equals the number of years a new hire will stay with the company.
let p of x equals the probability that a new hire will stay with the company x years.
